final_proof:
**Remark on the statement.** The types given in the statement contain obvious typos. Since $L:\mathbf D\to\mathbf C$, the opposite functor is $L^{\text{op}}:\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\to\mathbf C^{\text{op}}$ (given by $D\mapsto LD$, $f^{\text{op}}\mapsto (Lf)^{\text{op}}$). The hom bifunctor is $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-):\mathbf C^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C\to\mathbf{Set}$. These are the only types for which the composite is defined, and we prove the claim with them.

**Definitions used.**
* $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-)$: on objects, $(A,B)\mapsto \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(A,B)$. Take a morphism $(u^{\text{op}},g):(A,B)\to(A',B')$ of $\mathbf C^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C$, where $u:A'\to A$ and $g:B\to B'$ in $\mathbf C$. It is sent to the map $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(A,B)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(A',B')$, $h\mapsto g\circ h\circ u$.
* $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-):\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C\to\mathbf{Set}$: on objects, $(D,C)\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD,C)$. Take a morphism $(f^{\text{op}},g):(D,C)\to(D',C')$, where $f:D'\to D$ in $\mathbf D$ and $g:C\to C'$ in $\mathbf C$. It is sent to the map $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD,C)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD',C')$, $h\mapsto g\circ h\circ Lf$.
* The product $F\times G$ of functors acts componentwise on objects and morphisms. The composite $H\circ K$ sends each object or morphism $X$ to $H(KX)$.
* Two functors with the same domain and codomain are equal if and only if they agree on every object and every morphism.

**Step 1: $L^{\text{op}}$ is a functor $\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\to\mathbf C^{\text{op}}$.**
* *Sources and targets.* If $f^{\text{op}}:D\to D'$ in $\mathbf D^{\text{op}}$, then $f:D'\to D$. So $Lf:LD'\to LD$, and $(Lf)^{\text{op}}:LD\to LD'$ in $\mathbf C^{\text{op}}$, as required.
* *Identities.* $L^{\text{op}}(\mathrm{id}_D^{\text{op}})=(L\,\mathrm{id}_D)^{\text{op}}=\mathrm{id}_{LD}^{\text{op}}=\mathrm{id}_{LD}$ in $\mathbf C^{\text{op}}$.
* *Composition.* For composable $f^{\text{op}},g^{\text{op}}$ in $\mathbf D^{\text{op}}$ we have $f^{\text{op}}\circ g^{\text{op}}=(g\circ f)^{\text{op}}$. Hence
$L^{\text{op}}(f^{\text{op}}\circ g^{\text{op}})=(L(g\circ f))^{\text{op}}=(Lg\circ Lf)^{\text{op}}=(Lf)^{\text{op}}\circ(Lg)^{\text{op}}=L^{\text{op}}(f^{\text{op}})\circ L^{\text{op}}(g^{\text{op}})$.

It follows that $L^{\text{op}}\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}:\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C\to\mathbf C^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C$ is a functor. So $K:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-)\circ(L^{\text{op}}\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C})$ is a functor $\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C\to\mathbf{Set}$. It has the same domain and codomain as $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-)$.

**Step 2: the functors agree on objects.** For an object $(D,C)$ of $\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C$:
$K(D,C)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-)\big(L^{\text{op}}D,\ \operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}C\big)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-)(LD,C)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD,C)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-)(D,C).$

**Step 3: the functors agree on morphisms.** Let $(f^{\text{op}},g):(D,C)\to(D',C')$, with $f:D'\to D$ in $\mathbf D$ and $g:C\to C'$ in $\mathbf C$. Then
$(L^{\text{op}}\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C})(f^{\text{op}},g)=\big((Lf)^{\text{op}},g\big):(LD,C)\to(LD',C')$ in $\mathbf C^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C$, where $Lf:LD'\to LD$.

Apply the definition of the hom bifunctor with $u=Lf$. This shows that $K(f^{\text{op}},g)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-)\big((Lf)^{\text{op}},g\big)$ is the map $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD,C)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD',C')$, $h\mapsto g\circ h\circ Lf$. This map is exactly $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-)(f^{\text{op}},g)$: it has the same domain, codomain and rule.

**Conclusion.** The two functors $\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C\to\mathbf{Set}$ agree on all objects and all morphisms. Hence
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-)\circ(L^{\text{op}}\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}).\qquad\blacksquare$
